# Volume 2 — XXVI Around the Bend

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

The passing of Thomas Sowerby occurred as silently and modestly as the way he had conducted his existence. A compassionate, forbearing, and tireless caregiver was found in his wife. On occasion, Agatha had treated her Thomas with a degree of sharpness during his well days, whenever his lack of speed or submissiveness had irritated her; yet once sickness befell him, not a single voice proved quieter, no touch was more softly adept, and no watchfulness was borne with less grievance.
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0000 }

“Agatha, to me you have been a good wife,” he quietly remarked on one occasion, as she sat beside him in the twilight, cradling his pale, slender, aged hand within her own coarsened by labor. “A good wife. It grieves me that I do not leave you in a finer financial state; yet our offspring will care for you. Every one of them is an intelligent, competent child, taking right after their mother. A good mother . . . a good woman . . . .”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0001 }

His slumber came upon him after that, and when the pale daylight began edging over the sharp-topped fir trees down in the hollow the following morning, Thirza stepped quietly into the east gable to rouse Nell.
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0002 }

“Nell, Thomas Sowerby has passed away . . . the news was just delivered by their hired boy. I am heading down to Agatha immediately.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0003 }

The day following the burial of Thomas Sowerby, Thirza moved around Grey Shutters looking curiously distracted. At times she gazed at Nell, appearing as if she were about to speak, but she would then shake her head and press her lips together tightly. Following tea, she walked down to visit Mrs. Agatha; upon coming back, she made her way to the east gable, the place where Nell was marking school papers.
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0004 }

“In what condition is Mrs. Sowerby this evening?” inquired the second person.
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0005 }

“She is acting more peaceful and collected,” Thirza replied, taking a seat on Nell’s bed . . . an action that signified a rare state of emotional agitation, since according to Thirza’s set of domestic rules, resting on a bed once it had been prepared was an unforgivable breach of conduct. “However, she feels extremely solitary. Eliza was obliged to return home today . . . her boy is sick, so she believed she was unable to remain here any more.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0006 }

“After I complete these exercises, I am going to run downstairs and have a talk with Mrs. Sowerby for a bit,” Nell stated. “Tonight I had planned on studying a bit of Latin composition, although that is able to wait.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0007 }

“I guess Hugh Carrow will be attending college this autumn,” Thirza stated unevenly. “What would you think about going as well, Nell?”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0008 }

Nell raised her eyes, filled with surprise.
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0009 }

“Thirza, I would certainly enjoy that, yet it cannot be done.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0010 }

“I suppose we can arrange it. It has always been my belief that you ought to depart. My conscience was never at peace believing that my presence forced you to surrender everything.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0011 }

“However Thirza, not once have I regretted my decision to remain at home. My happiness has been complete . . . Oh, this two-year period that just passed was simply wonderful.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0012 }

“Oh, yes, I know you’ve been happy enough. But that isn't precisely the point. You should continue your schooling. You've set aside a sufficient amount to cover a single year at Wexcombe and the funds from the stock sale will manage a second year . . . and there are scholarships and similar awards you could earn.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0013 }

“Indeed, but my going is impossible, Thirza. It is true that your eyes have improved; nevertheless, I am unable to desert you with the twins. So much care is required by them.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0014 }

“I will not be by myself with them. That is the topic I intended to talk about with you. I spoke for a long time with Agatha this evening. Nell, she feels terribly upset regarding numerous matters. She is not left in a good financial state. Apparently, eight years back, they took out a mortgage on the farm to provide the youngest boy with a beginning when he moved west; and from that time on, they have barely managed to pay off anything beyond the interest. On top of that, Thomas’ illness has obviously been quite expensive, in various ways. Selling the farm will be necessary, and Agatha believes almost nothing will remain once the debts are paid. She states that residing with Eliza will be her only option, and the prospect of departing from Brierley is breaking her heart. Making new friends and finding new interests is not easy for a woman who is her age. And, Nell, while she was speaking of it, I had the idea that I might invite her to move in and reside with me, though I felt I should discuss it with you beforehand prior to mentioning it to her. If Agatha were residing alongside me, attending college would be possible for you. What is your reaction to this?”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0015 }

“It seems to me . . . almost . . . like . . . I’ve been given . . . the moon . . . without knowing . . . precisely . . . how to handle . . . it,” Nell uttered, bewildered. “However, regarding an invitation for Mrs. Sowerby to visit this place, Thirza, the choice rests with you. Is it your opinion . . . do you feel certain . . . that this would please you? A fine person and a helpful neighbor though Mrs. Sowerby is, . . . still . . .”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0016 }

“However, you are implying that she has her flaws? Naturally, she does; yet my preference would be to tolerate much greater defects instead of witnessing Agatha leave Brierley. Her absence would be missed by me terribly. Here, she is my sole intimate companion, and I would be at a loss in her absence. For forty-five years, our status has been that of neighbors without a single disagreement . . . albeit we approached one closely on the occasion when you attacked Mrs. Agatha because she referred to you as plain-looking and red-headed. Is that within your memory, Nell?”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0017 }

“I am certain that I do,” Nell remarked regretfully. “Individuals fail to erase such memories. At that instant, my hatred for poor Mrs. Agatha was immense!”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0018 }

“And furthermore, the ‘apology’ you offered to her. Indeed, Nell, you were quite difficult to deal with, in all honesty. Managing you left me feeling completely perplexed and confused. Obed had a superior understanding of you.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0019 }

“Obed grasped all of it,” Nell uttered quietly, in her habitual manner of speaking about him.
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0020 }

“Indeed, my view is that we might arrange things to prevent any friction whatsoever between Agatha and me. In my estimation, the conflict between two women living under one roof stems entirely from their attempts to use a single kitchen and stepping on one another's toes. Should Agatha move in, the north gable could serve as her sleeping quarters, and the spare room might just as easily become her kitchen, given that a spare room is totally unnecessary for us. Installing her stove and whatever furnishings she wishes to retain in that space would make her truly cozy and self-reliant. Naturally, her financial needs will be met...her children will take care of that...meaning my contribution is limited solely to shelter. Yes, Nell, speaking for myself, I am quite in favor of it.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0021 }

“Ask her, in that case,” Nell said without hesitation. “I personally would be extremely grieved if Mrs. Agatha were to depart.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0022 }

“And provided that she arrives,” Thirza went on, “it will be perfectly easy for you to attend college. I will have her for companionship, and she can handle the things for the twins that are beyond my ability, meaning there is absolutely no justification for you not going.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0023 }

That night, Nell engaged in a lengthy period of contemplation while seated at her window. Within her breast, happiness and sorrow contended with one another. Eventually . . . abruptly and without warning . . . she had arrived at the turn in the path; and beyond it lay college, accompanied by a century of iridescent expectations and dreams; yet Nell also understood that rounding this bend required her to abandon numerous precious delights. . . every small, humble responsibility and pastime that had become so cherished by her over the previous two years, which she had elevated into magnificence and joy through the passion she brought to them. Her school would have to be relinquished . . . and she possessed affection for each of her students, including those who were dull or misbehaved. Simply contemplating Cedric Stanhope caused her to question whether Wexcombe was truly such a magical name to evoke when all was said and done.
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0024 }

“Over these past two years, I’ve grown a great number of tiny roots,” Nell said to the moon, “and pulling them out will cause me a lot of pain. Even so, I believe leaving is the right choice, and, just as Thirza remarks, no valid reason exists for me to stay. I need to take out all my ambitions and give them a dusting.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0025 }

Nell submitted her notice of resignation twenty-four hours later; and Mrs. Agatha, following a candid conversation with Thirza, gladly agreed to the proposal of making her home at Grey Shutters. Nevertheless, she chose to stay in her personal residence during the summer season; because the farm would not be put up for sale until autumn and a great number of plans needed to be finalized.
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0026 }

“Living as distant from the thoroughfare as Grey Shutters was definitely something I had never considered,” Mrs. Agatha quietly uttered to herself. “However, Grey Shutters honestly appears less isolated than it once did . . . Nell receives plenty of visitors, while the twins keep things quite energetic. Regardless, I would prefer dwelling deep within a well to departing from Brierley.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0027 }

As these two choices became widely known, they quickly displaced the arrival of Mrs. Pettifer from local chatter. Wise individuals shook their heads regarding Thirza Abernethy’s reckless move to invite Mrs. Agatha to reside with her. Folks expressed the opinion that they would fail to coexist peacefully. Each was “too fond of their own way,” resulting in numerous gloomy forecasts, not one of which bothered the involved individuals in the slightest. Having reached an explicit and definite agreement regarding the duties and rights inherent to their updated living situation, they intended to adhere to them.
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0028 }

“I will not interfere with you, and you will not interfere with me,” Mrs. Agatha had stated firmly, “and regarding the twins, I will happily assist them as much as possible; however, I refuse to guarantee to respond to Robin’s inquiries, and that is final. I am no encyclopedia, and I am not a Philadelphia lawyer either. You will long for Nell because of that.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0029 }

“At times the replies Nell gave were nearly as strange as the inquiries Robin made,” Thirza remarked drily. “There is no doubt the twins are going to miss her; however, her prospects must not be given up for the sake of Robin’s desire to know things. Whenever he poses queries I am unable to reply to, I will simply inform him that young ones ought to be looked at rather than listened to. That is the manner in which I was raised, and I am not so sure but that it was quite as fine a method as every one of these modern ideas regarding child-rearing.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0030 }

“Well, the way Nell does things appears to have succeeded reasonably well where Robin is concerned,” Mrs. Sowerby remarked with a smile. “That’s what he is, a changed person.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0031 }

“He isn’t a bad little soul,” admitted Thirza. “I never thought I would become as attached to those children as I have. Robin wins you over somehow . . . and Lucy is a lovely child, even if she is . . . sort of . . . well, sort of . . .”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0032 }

“Unvarying? Precisely,” Mrs. Agatha offered. “Similar to a volume in which all pages are identical, it is precisely that. Lucy is going to become an amiable, dependable woman, yet she is never going to achieve anything extraordinary. Oh, that variety of people is pleasant to be around, although they are not quite as captivating as the alternative type.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0033 }

Hugh Carrow was likely the sole individual who experienced complete joy at the revelation that Nell had resigned. Her students, conversely, viewed the event as an absolute disaster. Going home, Annetta Bell fell into hysterics. To vent his emotions, Anthony Tulk engaged in two deliberate, unprovoked fights against fellow boys. All night long, Barbara Shaw wept. Cedric Stanhope boldly informed his grandmother that she should not count on him eating a single bowl of porridge over the coming week.
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0034 }

“Grandma, I can’t do it,” he said. “I’m really not sure if I’m able to eat a thing. It feels like a terrible lump is stuck in my throat. Had Jake Trask not been observing me, I’d have wept on my way back from school. I think I’m going to weep once I’m in bed. My eyes wouldn’t reveal it by tomorrow, would they? And I’d feel so much better. Regardless, eating porridge is impossible for me. Grandma, enduring this is going to require every bit of my mental fortitude, leaving me with none to tackle porridge. Oh Grandma, what I am going to do when my lovely teacher departs is beyond me. Milty Gammon wagers that Odette Pullen will be awarded the school. Miss Pullen is likely very pleasant, I imagine. Even so, I am certain her understanding of things won't match Miss Harcourt’s.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0035 }

Isolde held a similarly bleak perspective on the situation.
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0036 }

“The coming winter will be terribly lonely in this place,” she grieved, during an evening dusk as the moonlight poured down “airy silver” via the branches of the cherry tree and bathed the east gable in a gentle, ethereal glow where both girls sat conversing, Nell occupying her low rocking chair near the window, Isolde positioned cross-legged upon the bed. “Hugh and you will have departed . . . alongside the Waces. Port Marlow intends to issue a call to Mr. Wace, which he will naturally agree to. It is so unfair. I expect our pulpit will remain empty the entire winter, forcing us to endure an endless succession of candidating ministers . . . and a good portion of them will be useless.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0037 }

“I certainly trust they do not invite Mr. Baxter to come here from East Welby,” Nell stated with conviction. “Although he desires the position, his sermons are extremely somber. According to Mr. Bell, he belongs to the old school of clergy, yet Mrs. Sowerby claims that his sole issue is indigestion. Apparently, his spouse is not a particularly skilled cook, and Mrs. Sowerby remarks that whenever a gentleman is forced to consume sour bread two out of every three weeks, his religious views are certain to become warped. Mrs. Wace is deeply sorrowful regarding her departure. She mentions that everyone has shown her such warmth since her arrival as a newlywed that departing feels like parting from friends she has known her whole life. Furthermore, there is the matter of the infant's burial plot. She explains that she cannot imagine departing and abandoning it . . . it was such an exceptionally tiny creature and merely three months of age, and she expresses fear that it might yearn for its mother, even though she recognizes the folly of that thought and would never utter such a thing to Mr. Wace. She reveals that she has crept through the birch woods behind the parsonage almost every evening to reach the cemetery and sing a quiet lullaby to it. She disclosed all of this to me yesterday evening while I was up there placing a few of those early wild roses upon Obed’s grave. I assured her that for as long as I remain in Brierley I will place blossoms upon the infant's grave and whenever I am elsewhere I felt confident that . . .”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0038 }

“I promised to undertake it,” Isolde offered with enthusiasm. “I certainly shall. Furthermore, I shall place them upon Obed’s grave as well, on your account, Nell.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0039 }

“Oh, I appreciate that. I intended to request that you do so. And also regarding little Dinah Wren’s? Kindly remember hers as well. You see, my thoughts and dreams have dwelt on little Dinah Wren to such an extent that she feels remarkably actual to me. My mind envisions her, over there within her tiny garden inside that refreshing, quiet, verdant nook; and I entertain a notion that were I able to slip back to that place on a certain spring evening, right at the magical moment between daylight and nightfall, and walk on tiptoe so gently up the hill of beeches that my treads would not startle her, I might discover the garden exactly as it used to exist, completely fragrant with lilies of June and early-blooming roses, with the small dwelling past it entirely covered in vines; and little Dinah Wren would be present, possessing her gentle eyes, with her dark hair ruffled by the breeze, walking around, placing her fingertips beneath the chins of the lilies and sharing secrets in whispers with the roses; and I would advance, oh, extremely quietly, and extend my hands and speak to her, ‘Little Dinah Wren, won’t you let me be your playmate, for I love the roses too?’ And the two of us would sit on the ancient bench and converse a bit and daydream a bit, or simply remain wonderfully quiet alongside one another. And after that the moon would ascend and I would survey my surroundings . . . and neither Dinah Wren nor the small vine-draped home nor any roses would be present . . . merely a neglected former garden dotted with June lilies among the wild grass, alongside the breeze lamenting, oh, so mournfully among the cherry trees. And I would be unable to tell if it was genuine or whether I had merely envisioned everything.” Isolde crept upward and positioned her back against the bed's headboard. Whenever the person sharing your dusk hour uttered such eerie statements, it was preferable to prevent yourself from imagining that something was lurking behind you.
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0040 }

“I fear the Improvement Society will collapse once you and Hugh have both left,” she observed mournfully.
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0041 }

“There isn’t any danger of that,” Nell rejoined with vigor, returning to real-world matters from her reveries. “It has been built on too solid a foundation to fail, particularly as the elderly folk are getting so excited over it. Consider the work they are putting into their yards and pathways during these summer months. Furthermore, I intend to keep an eye out for ideas while at Wexcombe, and during the coming winter I am going to compose an essay about it to mail across. Stop looking at the world so pessimistically, Isolde. Nor should you resent this brief moment of joy and triumph that I am experiencing right now. At a future time, when my departure arrives, my mood will be far from joyful.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0042 }

“It is fine for you to feel happy . . . you are heading to college where you will enjoy yourself and form plenty of wonderful new friendships.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0043 }

“I trust that I will form new friendships,” Nell remarked with contemplation. “The prospects of creating fresh acquaintances assist in rendering life exceedingly intriguing. However, regardless of the quantity of companions I acquire, they will not ever hold the same fondness for me as my former ones . . . particularly a particular female possessing dark eyes and facial indentations. Are you able to deduce her identity, Isolde?”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0044 }

“However, Wexcombe will have a great number of smart girls,” Isolde sighed, “whereas I am merely an unintelligent little girl from the country who occasionally says ‘I seen’. . . even if I actually am aware of the correct phrasing whenever I pause to consider it. Oh well, naturally the previous two years were truly far too enjoyable to endure forever. I am aware of a person who is pleased that you will be attending Wexcombe regardless. Nell, I shall pose a query to you . . . a grave query. Do not become angry and please give a grave reply. Is Hugh of any importance to you?”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0045 }

“Just like a friend and not at all how you imply,” Nell stated with composure and firmness, genuinely believing in her own truthfulness as she spoke.
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0046 }

Isolde let out a sigh. Somehow, she desired that Nell’s response had been different.
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0047 }

“Are you never going to get married, Nell?”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0048 }

“Maybe . . . eventually . . . whenever the ideal person comes along,” Nell uttered, looking up into the moonlight with a dreamy smile.
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0049 }

“Yet by what means can you be certain when the correct individual is actually encountered by you?” Isolde continued to press.
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0050 }

“Oh, he would be recognized by me . . . I would be alerted by an inner feeling. The nature of my ideal is known to you, Isolde.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0051 }

“However, a person's values occasionally undergo a transformation.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0052 }

“My own will not change. Furthermore, it would be impossible for me to feel affection for a man who failed to satisfy it.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0053 }

“What if you never meet him?”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0054 }

“In that case, I will pass away as an old maid,” she replied in a spirited manner. “I am inclined to think it is far from being the most difficult way to die.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0055 }

“Oh, I guess dying would not be very difficult; living as an old maid is what I would dismally dislike,” Isolde remarked, without meaning to be funny. “Even though being an old maid would not bother me greatly if I could resemble Miss Rosalind. However, I could never manage that. By the time I reach forty-five, I will be terribly stout. And whereas a slender old maid might possess some romance, a stout one could not possibly have any. Oh, listen to this, Nelson Atkins asked Opal Pettigrew to marry him three weeks back. Opal related the whole story to me. She claims she had no plan whatsoever to accept him, since whoever marries him must reside with his parents; yet Opal claims his proposal was so completely lovely and romantic that it totally overwhelmed her. Nevertheless, not wishing to act hastily, she requested a week for deliberation; and a couple of days afterward, she attended a Sewing Circle gathering at his mother's house, where a volume titled ‘The Complete Guide to Etiquette’ was situated on the parlor table. Opal stated that she just could not express what she felt when she discovered, within a chapter labeled ‘The Deportment of Courtship and Marriage,’ the exact proposal Nelson had delivered, verbatim. She returned home and composed a thoroughly blistering rejection to him; and she claims his father and mother have taken turns guarding him continuously since then because they dread he will drown himself in the river; however, Opal claims there is no need for their fear; because the Deportment of Courtship and Marriage explained the proper conduct for a turned-down suitor, and drowning is not mentioned there. Furthermore, she claims Wilbur Blair is truly wasting away on account of her, but she is utterly powerless in the situation.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0056 }

Nell shifted with a gesture of impatience.
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0057 }

“I am reluctant to admit it . . . it feels terribly disloyal . . . but, really, I no longer care for Opal Pettigrew. I was fond of her during our time at school and Regent’s together . . . although certainly not as much as you and Odette. However, throughout this past year at Delford she appears so changed . . . so . . . so . . .”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0058 }

“I know,” Isolde nodded. “It’s the Pettigrew in her coming out . . . she cannot help it. Mrs. Sowerby claims that if a Pettigrew girl ever contemplated anything other than the boys, it was never evident in her walk and conversation. She speaks of nothing except boys and the compliments they give her, as well as how mad they all are for her at Delford. And the odd part is, they really are, too . . .” This was admitted somewhat resentfully by Isolde. “When I observed her in Mr. Blair’s store last night, she whispered to me that she had just secured a new ‘mash.’ Because I knew she was eager to be asked, I wouldn’t ask her who he was. Well, I suppose it is what Opal always desired. You recall how even as a little girl she constantly stated she intended to possess dozens of beaus when she reached adulthood and enjoy the very gayest time possible prior to settling down. She is so unlike Odette, isn’t she? Odette is a girl who is so nice, sensible, and lady-like.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0059 }

“Sweet old Odette is a treasure,” concurred Nell, “however,” she continued, bending toward the fleshy, pitted small hand suspended above her cushion to give it a affectionate stroke, “no one can truly compare to my very own Isolde. Can you recall that night of our initial encounter, Isolde, when we ‘pledged’ undying companionship within your garden? I believe we have honored that ‘vow’ . . . not a single disagreement or even a chilly distance has ever come between us. The surge of excitement that swept through me on the day you confessed your affection for me will remain with me forever. Throughout my youth, my heart was so desolate and deprived. Only now am I starting to understand the true extent of that deprivation and solitude. No one had any regard for me or wished to be burdened by my presence. Had it not been for my peculiar little world of fantasy, in which I pictured all the companions and devotion I desired, I would have been wretched. Yet arriving at Grey Shutters altered every single thing. Following that, I encountered you. The significance of your comradeship to me is beyond your knowing. Right at this moment, my dear, I wish to express my gratitude for the steadfast and genuine fondness you have constantly bestowed upon me.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0060 }

“And forever, forever I will,” weeping, Isolde uttered. “I will not ever care for any person . . . any girl . . . even half so much as I care for you. And should I actually wed and give birth to a small daughter of my own, I intend to call her Nell.”
{: #nw-v02-c26-p0061 }
